title: Sinigang
subtitle: filipino sour tamarind soup
excerpt: Sinigang is a Filipino sour soup made with pork or chicken, vegetables, and tamarind for sourness. It is warming, tangy, and deeply savoury, eaten as an everyday family meal. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Sinigang is one of the most eaten dishes in the Philippines. The souring agent varies by region; tamarind is the most common. Other versions use green mango, guava, or calamansi.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Filipino sour soup made with meat and vegetables, soured with tamarind. One of the most beloved everyday dishes in Filipino cooking.
A sour paste made from the pulp of tamarind pods. It is the traditional souring agent in sinigang and many Filipino dishes.

content.text: Place the pork and water in a stockpot. Bring to a boil and skim off any foam that rises to the surface.
Add the onion wedges. Reduce to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes.
Add the carrot and aubergine. Cook for 10 minutes until just tender.
Stir in the tamarind paste and fish sauce. Taste. Adjust the sourness with more tamarind and the saltiness with more fish sauce.
Add the spinach. Stir once and remove from the heat. The spinach will wilt in the hot broth.
Ladle into bowls and serve immediately with steamed white rice.

attrs.problem: The broth is not sour enough.
attrs.solution: Add more tamarind paste a tablespoon at a time. The sour level is a matter of personal preference; Filipinos tend to make it quite tart.
Simmer for longer. Pork loin can toughen if the heat is too high. Keep the broth at a gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil.

content.text: Sinigang is one of the most eaten soups in the Philippines. It is a comfort food eaten throughout the year. The dish varies significantly by region and by what souring agent is used. Tamarind powder packets are widely used in Filipino homes as a shortcut. The soup is always served with steamed white rice.
